```{r setup, include=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
# The walkthrough runs on a simulated dataset that is not shipped with the package (misc/notebook/prepare_sim_dataset.R
# builds it). The chunks are evaluated only when that file is given (misc/notebook/render_walkthrough.sh renders the
# executed Markdown copy in vignettes/); the vignette build evaluates nothing.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = file.exists(params$sim.file), purl = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      message = FALSE, warning = TRUE, comment = "")
```

Cacoa compares samples (patients, donors, replicates) across conditions. The analysis is organized around one
**model**: a formula with the condition of interest and the covariates to adjust for, and one **contrast**, the
comparison being made. The model is set once and every analysis uses it: expression shifts per cell type,
composition, differential expression, cell density and the cluster-free analyses.

The recommended order is

1. `Cacoa$new()` with the sample metadata.
2. `cao$checkDesign()`: is the planned comparison identifiable from the metadata alone?
3. `cao$screenCovariates()` and `cao$plotSampleDistances()`: which covariates are associated with sample-level
   variation, in which cell types, and what does the sample structure look like?
4. `cao$setModel()`: the model and the contrast used from here on.
5. `cao$estimateExpressionShiftMagnitudes()` and the other analyses.
6. `cao$checkSensitivity()`: does the result depend on the covariate set or on single samples?

This walkthrough uses a **simulated** dataset: 20 samples, 10 treated and 10 control, and 9 cell types. Expression
differences between the arms were planted with a known strength per cell type: strong in `IN-SST`, `IN-PV` and `L2/3`;
moderate in `OPC`, `L5/6-CC` and `AST-PP`; weak in `AST-FB`; none in `Microglia` and `Neu-NRGN`. The simulated arms also differ in composition (not planted on
purpose, but present): `L2/3` and `L5/6-CC` are about half as frequent in the treated arm, `IN-PV` and `IN-SST` almost
twice as frequent, `AST-FB` and `OPC` somewhat more frequent. A sample `age` was added as a covariate: the treated arm is older on average, but age has
no effect on expression in the simulation. The same code runs on any Conos or Seurat object with a sample metadata
table.

```{r libs, purl=FALSE}
library(cacoa)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Load data

The sample metadata is a data frame with one row per sample (row names are the sample names) and one column per
covariate.

```{r load, purl=FALSE}
sim <- readRDS(params$sim.file)
head(sim$sample.meta)
```

```{r construct, message=TRUE, purl=FALSE}
cao <- Cacoa$new(sim$con, sample.metadata = sim$sample.meta, cell.groups = sim$cell.groups, sample.per.cell = sim$sample.per.cell,
                 n.cores = params$n.cores)
```

The constructor reports which metadata columns can serve as covariates and which cannot (sample identifiers,
constant or mostly missing columns, too many levels). Options shared by all methods are set once; explicit arguments
of a method call still win. `plot.params` holds defaults for the embedding plots.

```{r options, purl=FALSE}
cao$setOptions(n.permutations = 499, seed = 1)
cao$plot.params <- list(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.3, font.size = 3)
```

## Check the design

Before fitting anything, the metadata alone tells whether the comparison can be adjusted for the other covariates:
associations between covariates, balance of the arms over them, aliasing, degrees of freedom and the number of
distinct permutations the design allows.

```{r check-design, purl=FALSE}
cao$checkDesign(test = "treatment")
```

```{r plot-design-balance, fig.width=4, fig.height=3.5, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotDesign("balance")
```

The treated arm is older on average, so age should be adjusted for; the check suggests comparing the adjusted and
the unadjusted result, which `checkSensitivity()` does below.

## Screen covariates

The screen tests every usable covariate against the sample-to-sample expression distances of each cell type, alone
(marginal) and adjusted for the other covariates (partial). Two summary columns come first: all cell types combined
and the cell-type composition. The last column is a global test over the cell types. The screen ends with a suggested
model; it is not applied automatically.

```{r screen, purl=FALSE}
cao$screenCovariates(n.permutations = 199)
```

```{r plot-screen, fig.width=8, fig.height=3, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotCovariateScreen()
```

```{r plot-varpart, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotVariancePartition(c("treatment", "age"))
```

Treatment explains a large part of the between-sample variation in the planted cell types and none in `Microglia`
and `Neu-NRGN`; age explains nothing, as simulated.

### Sample maps

`plotSampleDistances()` draws the samples in two dimensions (MDS of the sample distances) in one of three spaces:
`"expression"` (one cell type, or all cell types combined when `cell.type` is not given), `"pseudobulk"` (all cells of a
sample pooled) and `"composition"` (cell-type proportions). The subtitle gives the chance-corrected R² and permutation
p-value of each color and shape variable on its own, the screen's marginal numbers (its summary lines print the
partial ones where the degrees of freedom allow them). No model is needed.

```{r plot-sample-maps, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.6, purl=FALSE}
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotSampleDistances(color.by = "treatment"),
                   cao$plotSampleDistances(space = "composition", color.by = "treatment"),
                   cao$plotSampleDistances(space = "composition", color.by = "age"), ncol = 3)
```

Over all cell types the two arms are apart (adj. R² 0.13); in the composition they are further apart (0.44), the
unplanned composition differences described above. Age structures neither.

## Set the model

`test` names the variable to test. For a two-level factor the contrast compares its two levels; the reference level
is chosen automatically (here `control`, matched by name) and `test = "treatment: control vs treated"` would reverse
it. The printout states the contrast, the adjustment set and the permutation scheme.

```{r set-model, purl=FALSE}
cao$setModel(~ treatment + age, test = "treatment")
```

## Expression shifts per cell type

For every cell type, the question is which cell types changed, and how much. Each sample's cells of the type are pooled
into a profile, and two things are estimated:

- **Is there a change?** For every gene, the contrast of its profile across the samples is divided by its standard
  error (sampling noise of the profile plus donor-level variation), and the gene z-scores are combined adaptively, so
  that both a strong change in a few genes and a weak change in many are detected (`statistic = "gsd"`, the default).
  Permutations of the sample labels give the p-values, adjusted across cell types (`padj`).
- **How big is the change?** The sample-to-sample distances of the type are modeled with the formula above, which
  gives three effects:

| effect | meaning |
|---|---|
| `shift` | the arms differ in a common direction: squared distance between the arm means relative to the within-arm spread |
| `var`   | the treated arm is more (or less) heterogeneous than the control arm: log2 ratio of the arm dispersions, at equal cell numbers |
| `total` | treated samples are farther from control samples than control samples are from each other |

The normalized shift is comparable across cell types and does not depend on the numbers of cells; `var` is tested by
the distance model.

```{r shifts, purl=FALSE}
res <- cao$estimateExpressionShiftMagnitudes()
res
```

```{r plot-shifts, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.8, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotExpressionShiftMagnitudes()
```

All seven cell types with a planted change are called, including the weak one (`AST-FB`), and the two without a
planted change are not. The sizes follow the planted strengths only roughly (`L5/6-CC`, planted as moderate, lies
above `IN-SST`): the normalized shift measures the change relative to each type's own within-arm spread.

Cell types are ordered by the size of the shift; filled points have a significant change. The gray band is the range
of the shift with shuffled labels (what noise alone gives). Significance and size answer different questions: a small
but consistent change can be significant, and a large estimate based on few or heterogeneous samples may not be. The
jackknife intervals (`show.ci = TRUE`) show how firmly the samples determine the size; they are not a test. The genes
changed at a gene-level FDR can be added as a margin (`show.genes = TRUE`); their number depends on the numbers of
samples and cells, so it is a cross-check rather than a ranking.

```{r plot-shifts-full, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotExpressionShiftMagnitudes(show.ci = TRUE, show.genes = TRUE)
```

The dispersion change, on the same layout:

```{r plot-var, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.8, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotExpressionShiftMagnitudes(effect = "var")
```

### Behind one cell type

`plotShiftDetail()` shows the sample-level picture of the distance model for one cell type: the samples in the adjusted
distance space, the distribution of pair distances within and between the arms, and the per-sample dispersion.

```{r plot-shift-detail, fig.width=12, fig.height=3.8, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotShiftDetail("IN-SST")
```

`plotSampleInfluence()` shows how much each sample changes the shift estimate of each cell type when it is left out,
in units of the jackknife standard error.

```{r plot-influence, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotSampleInfluence()
```

## Robustness

The shifts are re-estimated without adjustment, with the current model, and with the covariates proposed by the screen,
and two questions are answered per cell type. The size (the distance-model magnitude, as in the main result): near zero (inside the noise band of shuffled labels),
stable, changing by more than half, sign depending on the model, or driven by one sample. The significance (by gsd, the
test of the main result, refitted under each model): significant in all, some or none of the models.

```{r sensitivity, purl=FALSE}
cao$checkSensitivity(n.permutations = 199)
```

```{r plot-sensitivity, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotSensitivity()
```

Adjusting for age changes nothing here: the seven changed cell types are significant with and without it, and the
two unchanged ones in neither model.

## Sample structure after the model

Once a model is set, the maps can also be drawn with its covariates removed (`values = "adjusted"`, or `"both"` side by
side): a covariate that was adjusted for should no longer structure the samples.

```{r plot-sample-distances, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotSampleDistances(cell.type = "IN-SST", values = "both", color.by = "age", shape.by = "test")
```

## Differential expression and composition on the same model

The stored model is used by the per-cell-type differential expression, by the compositional analysis and by the
cell density analysis, and is recorded with each result.

```{r de, purl=FALSE}
de <- cao$estimateDEPerCellType(test = "limma-voom", min.cell.count = 5)
head(de[["IN-SST"]]$res[, c("Gene", "log2FoldChange", "pvalue", "padj", "CellFrac")])
```

```{r plot-n-de, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5, purl=FALSE}
cao$plotNumberOfDEGenes()
```

Compositional changes are tested on the same contrast (cell-type loadings of the treated versus the control arm):

```{r loadings, fig.width=5, fig.height=5, purl=FALSE}
cao$estimateCellLoadings()
cao$plotCellLoadings()
```

## Cluster-free analyses

Cell density is compared between the arms in every cell's neighborhood with the same model. The unit is a kNN
neighborhood of the cell graph: the cell, its graph neighbors and, up to a minimum size, their neighbors, sized by
default to the larger of 100 cells and 10 cells per sample (`k`). Each sample's share of the neighborhood's cells is
tested on the log scale, and the statistic is then averaged over each cell and its graph neighbors under every
permutation alike (`post = "averaged"`), an exact test of a slightly larger unit that borrows strength from the
neighbors without inflating the error. The per-cell statistics are strongly dependent and permutation p-values are
floored at 1 / (permutations + 1), so the maps are adjusted by a pooled permutation false-discovery rate
(`adjust.method = "perm-fdr"`): the number of cells beyond a threshold under the permutations, pooled over all cells,
against the observed number. The heat-kernel density (`smoothing = "heat"`, width in cells with `target.size`),
Benjamini-Hochberg on per-cell p-values (`"bh"`) and the familywise max-statistic adjustment (`"max-t"`) remain
available. The cluster-free expression shifts test the contrast in the same kNN neighborhoods with the same
post-processing and adjustment.

Before the density test, the neighborhood unit is checked: how many cells each sample contributes to a unit, how large
the units are, and how pure they are against the annotation.

```{r neighbourhoods}
nb <- cao$checkNeighbourhoods(verbose = FALSE); cat(nb$text, "\n")
```

```{r density, fig.width=14, fig.height=4.5, purl=FALSE}
cao$estimateCellDensity(method = "graph")
cao$estimateDiffCellDensity(type = "permutation")
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotDiffCellDensity(what = "effect", contours = "L2/3"), cao$plotDiffCellDensity(adjust = FALSE),
                   cao$plotDiffCellDensity(adjust = TRUE), ncol = 3)
```

Left to right: the effect (the log2 fold change of the density per cell), the unadjusted z-scores (the signed tail z of the
per-cell p-values of the pooled permutation null, calibrated and not floored at 1 / (permutations + 1)) and the
adjusted z-scores (the tail z of the FDR q-values). The color range of a z map is the 99.5 % quantile of the absolute
z-scores, so a few extreme cells do not wash out the map. The density map agrees with the loadings: `L2/3` and
`L5/6-CC` are depleted in the treated arm, `IN-PV`, `IN-SST` and `OPC` enriched. The expression shifts show the planted
cell types, again as the shift magnitude, the unadjusted and the adjusted z-scores (one-sided):

```{r cluster-free-shifts, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.8, purl=FALSE}
cao$estimateClusterFreeExpressionShifts(n.permutations = 99)
cao$plotClusterFreeExpressionShifts(font.size = 3)
```

The map also calls the microglia, which carry no planted change (and part of `Neu-NRGN`), while the per-type test
does not (adjusted p 0.68). The three types form one cloud on the graph: 40 % of the cells in a microglial neighborhood
belong to other types, mostly `AST-FB` (21 %) and the strongly changed `L5/6-CC` and `L2/3` (9 %). The map reports a
neighborhood effect there, the risk of any test that borrows neighboring cells across cell-type boundaries; the
per-type test and `checkNeighbourhoods()` (purity of the units) are the checks.

Both cluster-free maps are summarized per cell type by an exact group-level permutation test: the mean per-cell
statistic of the type is compared with the same mean under the permutations shared by all cells, so the dependence
between neighboring cells is carried along, and the result is adjusted across types. This gives a verdict per type
where the per-cell map is too sparse to call single cells (a Cauchy combination of the cells' p-values is the
alternative, `method = "cauchy"`).

```{r cluster-free-summary, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, purl=FALSE}
cao$estimateClusterFreeSummary("cell.density")
cao$estimateClusterFreeSummary("cluster.free.expr.shifts")
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotClusterFreeSummary("cell.density"), cao$plotClusterFreeSummary("cluster.free.expr.shifts"), ncol = 2)
```

The density summary recovers the composition differences of the simulation and the shift summary the planted cell
types. `Microglia` is also called by the shift summary although nothing was planted there: its neighborhoods border
`AST-FB`, whose frequency differs between the arms, so the neighborhood profiles shift with the composition. The
per-cell-type test above, which pools the cells of a type, puts `Microglia` at zero; a neighborhood-level expression
test cannot separate the two.

## Functional interpretation

The DE tables feed a gene set enrichment analysis per cell type (GSEA on GO biological processes, through
clusterProfiler), and the enriched terms are summarized by grouping related terms: terms are first clustered by the genes
they share, then by their enrichment pattern across cell types, and each cluster is labeled by its most frequent words.
The simulated genes have no annotation, so the chunks below are shown but not run; see the real-data examples in
`examples/` for executed versions.

```{r ontology, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
cao$estimateOntology(type = "GSEA", org.db = org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db)
cao$plotOntologyHeatmapCollapsed(name = "GSEA", genes = "up", n = 25, clust.method = "ward.D")
cao$plotOntology(cell.type = "IN-SST", name = "GSEA", genes = "up")
```
